speechtext: On the Orders of the Day :

Would the Minister of Militia and Defence kindly inform the House when the papers relative to the taking over of the Ross rifle factory will be brought down, and whether a statement will shortly be made by the Government with reference to the manufacture of rifles in Canada?
The Order in Council providing for the taking over of the Ross rifle factory will be brought down to-morrow.
Will the Government be in a position to make a statement with regard to the manufacture of rifles in this country at an early date?

Appraisers are now taking an inventory of the Ross rifle factory. The Government is using the greatest possible dispatch in having the necessary specifications and patterns prepared for the making of a new rifle.
Is the factory at present closed?
A certain number of men are employed in the taking of the inventory, but there is no manufacturing going on at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will inform my hon. friend to-morrow.

Would the Minister of Militia and Defence kindly inform us what the policy of the Government is with regard to the salaries of inside civil servants who have enlisted? It will be remembered that when these civil servants were invited to offer themselves for overseas service they were given the assurance that their salaries would not be lower than what they were receiving in the service, and I understand that the military pay has been supplemented

in certain cases in accordance with that assurance. Those civil servants who enlisted two years ago would now be getting, if they had remained in the service, their regular statutory increase, and I wish to know whether allowance is made for that when they are given their military pay.

The question which my hon. friend raises was brought to my attention this morning,. My own view is that these civil servants should get the regular statutory increase, and the matter is being looked into with a view to ascertaining the exact position.

I should like to ask a question with regard to separation allowances. in the case of civil servants who have enlisted. A return was laid upon the Table the other day giving the names of a number of members of this House who had been appointed to different positions in the Militia, some of them occupying the position of colonel, and who were receiving their sessional indemnity, the salary attached to their military position, and separation allowance as well. I am told that in the case of at least some civil servants who have enlisted the separation allowance has been refused. I would ask whether that is the case, and if so, why a distinction is made to the prejudice of the members of the Civil Service.
I have not heard that there has been any discrimination against either members of Parliament or civil servants in respect of enlistment in the overseas forces.

There is a case within my own personal knowledge of the wife of a civil servant who was refused a separation allowance. She was informed by the Department of Militia and Defence that no separation allowance was granted in the case of a civil servant. We also know from the return that was laid on the Table the other day that separation allowances have been granted to the wives of members of Parliament, who were receiving both military pay and their sessional indemnities.

I should be glad if my hon. friend would give me the name of the person he has in mind, so that we may look into the case, and I shall then be able to answer intelligently the question which my hon. friend raises. Personally I do not see why any civil servant in the overseas forces should not be entitled to a separation allowance for his wife.

It might be a little objectionable to give the name, because sometimes when a civil servant complains he does not possibly receive the treatment from the officials which he otherwise would receive. But if my hon. friend will make inquiry in the department he will find the statement which I have made to be correct, and if he does not find it to be correct, I shall gladly furnish him with the name.
I will make inquiry, but I can assure my hon. friend that no soldier will be discriminated against for advancing his claim.

I should like to direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to the following despatch from Stellairtion, which appears in the Halifax HeraJld1:
Stellarton, April 20.-There is much excitement in this town as to future work in the Acadia Coal company's mines. This seems a peculiar statement when anything black is saleable as fuel. The company have now about 20,000 tons in bank. Cars are not obtainable, it is claimed, to ship this to customers. It is rumored that there is serious trouble between the company and the management of the Intercolonial.
This company, being on the line to Sydney, supplies the larger share of the tonnage on the eastern division. Report says that the Canadian Pacific pays over $5 a ton to this company and to the Greenwood company, and that they guarantee cars to take their tonnage. The Canadian government import coal at a cost of $7 per ton at least. The company says its wages to the men are dependent on the price it gets from the I. C. R., who take one-third of its product.
Further rumour says that Scotia is having a price 50 cents in excess of that offered and that they have limited the quantity that it will require from that company. All the miners want is no discrimination against this company and the going price, so that thereby they can secure the going wage.
I am advised that the Minister of Railways has offered this company $4.25 a ton for coal, while the Canadian Pacific Railway is paying this and other companies $5.25 a ton, and I am also informed that the minister paid $9.25 for coal purchased in the United States and delivered at Halifax. What is the position of my hon. friend with regard to this matter?

We have made no contract yet with this company, but we have offered them the same price at which we are buying

from other companies. I have not heard anything with reference to a shortage of cars, but I will take the matter up, and if the coal is shipped there will certainly be ears to ship it in.

I was not referring to the non-shipment of coal, although it is well known in Nova Scotia that there are 20,000 tons of coal banked up at the Acadia mines through the failure of the Intercolonial to supply cans. What I wanted to know is why the Minister of Railways was haggling with this company and offering them $4.25 a ton for coal when the Canadian Pacific Railway was paying for the same quality $5.25 'a ton, and when my hon. friend had paid $9.25 a ton for American coal delivered at Halifax.
We neveT paid $9.25 a ton for coal delivered at Halifax.
It was so stated by my hon. friend himself in this House in February last.
But we offered this company and other companies more money than their contract called for, and they did not fill their contract.
What are you going to do about it?
That is a matter for us to settle, not you.
It is not altogether a matter for my hon. friend to settle, but for the people of this country. The Minister of Railways does not own the country yet as he will find out.

As the subject of coal has
been mentioned, I desire to call the attention of the Government to the fact that during the past winter, and even up to the present time, in the city of St. John where a great deal of anthracite coal is burned which can only be obtained from the United States, people have been obliged to pay an enormous price for that article, as much,
I am informed, as $13.75 a ton. We are told that the reason for -these high prices is that coal has to be brought to St. John by vessel and that there is a great scarcity in tonnage, and therefore freights are very high. I do not dispute that; my object in rising is to call the attention of the Government to the fact, which I have brought before this House on many occasions, that there is a great scarcity of tonnage for carrying the water-borne freight of Canada. The matter is a very serious one indeed for those who have to use American coal transported by water. I would ask the Government if any steps have been taken by them to encourage the building of ships, more especially wooden ships, not merely to- engage in ocean transportation but for coast transportation, which is vital to the people of oui country. I was glad to notice the other day that the authority in the United States charged with these matters had decided to give an order for one thousand wooden vessels.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. member that there is no subject before the Chair. I wish he would submit his question.
Having made my preliminary observations. I desire to ask if any steps have been taken by the Government for the building of vessels in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Orders have been placed by the Imperial Government with Canadian shipyards for some twenty-two vessels. I understand that further orders _ for eight vessels are under consideration. This will involve a tonnage of 175,000 tons. The effect is that all the shipbuilding plants of Canada have sufficient orders to carry them well into the middle of 1918. We have given attention to the question of shipbuilding, because, as the hon. gentleman says, it is vital at this time. The more ships we can build, the more the existing shipping of the world will be available for the transportation to our Allies of commodities of all kinds. Some time ago I took up this question with the Imperial Munitions Board acting for the Imperial Government here, as to what is to be done towards building wooden ships for the purpose of transporting the products of Canada to Great Britain in order to assist in the situation which has become so acute by reason of the submarine menace. The representative of the Minister of Shipping, Mr. Perry, has been looking into the question, both on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of Canada. Recently I offered, on behalf of the Government, to find money on this side of the ocean, to the amount of $10,000,000, to place the Imperial Government in funds for the construction and purchase of wooden ships in Canada. The matter is now under consideration, and I am of the opirtion that orders for a considerable tonnage of wooden ships will be placed in Canada through the Imperial Munitions Board. These, of course,' will be of service to transport our products to the United Kingdom, and will also ease the general shipping situation to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. W. CROTHERS (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Perhaps I should add a word in answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) on the subject of coal. He will be aware that an order in Council was passed last November, concerning the prices of fuel, clothing, and food. Under that order we have sent out questionaires to all the known coal dealers in Canada, and to these

we have received answers under oath. I have not the figures before me, but, speaking from memory, I think there is no return showing any such price as my hon. friend has stated. Speaking further from memory, I think the order contains a provision compelling dealers to sell any of the products referred to at a reasonable and just price; so that, if any one in the city of St. John feels aggrieved at the price charged for coal, with the consent, of the Attorney General of the province he can prosecute the dealer for demanding a higher price than is reasonable and just.

I disclaim having suggested that the coal dealers of St. John were asking more than a fair price. What I said was that the excessive freight which they were compelled to pay for water transportation is alleged to be the cause of the very high price. I am sorry to learn from the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) that the Government itself has taken no steps to build ships in Canada but is relying upon the Imperial Government.

I wish to ask the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Edward Kemp) a question in regard to the position of Canadian Prisoners of War in Germany. I have a letter from one of these prisoners who states that after these men were detained there was some difficulty about their pay being made available through governmental sources for the purpose of enabling them to get food, and that as a consequence the parents and friends of the prisoners contributed, as we all know they did, to send food to them. It was stated in the press not long ago that some restriction was imposed on the rights of the relatives and friends of prisoners to send them clothing or food and the matter upon which I want information is: What is the Government doing now? Is it possible for the Government to utilize the pay of these men, which is running on, I presume, although they are prisoners, for the purpose of enabling them to get food through governmental sources, or what provision is being made now for them in view of the fact that private parties are prevented from sending them sustenance?

The question
which my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) raises, I think, has reference to the Red

Cross Society's shipments to Great Britain. I am not prepared to make a statement at the moment but I shall endeavour to do so to-morrow and in the meantime I shall make further inquiry.
On Thursday last the Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid) promised to bring down a statement in regard to coal contracts which I asked the minister about a short time ago and he has not done , so.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. B. McCOIG (West Kent) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, on account of the great shortage in the bean crop in Canada during 1916, and the urgent need in this country for this article, in the interest of the consumer and producer, beans for seed purposes should be allowed to come into Canada duty free.
He said: Mr. Speaker, my chief reason for moving this resolution is the great shortage in the bean crop in the southwestern part of Ontario. We have been unfortunate in our attempts to get seed for the different crops which the farmers are desirous of putting in. This is particularly true of the bean crop, which last season was a complete failure in the counties of Essex, Kent and Lambton, and
in parts of Elgin county. We have had to get the seed from the United States. The seed which was brought in last year from the United States matured about two weeks earlier than the home-grown seed, and the farmers who were fortunate enough to get seed from the United States had a great advantage over those who used home-grown seed. They are anxious, therefore, to get as much of the seed this year from the state of Michigan as they possibly can. A request to this effect has been made in a petition which, I understand, has been forwarded to the Government, and the demand has been voiced also by farmers' associations in the county of Kent. In view of the high price of seed at the present time, a greatly increased production during this year will result if the Government can see its way clear to allow the farmers to have their bean seed brought in free of duty and free of war tax. The Prime Minister and the other members of the Government, as well as the citizens of Canada, are particularly anxious that every farmer shall produce as much as he possibly can, and if satisfactory results in this respect are to be obtained, it will be absolutely necessary to get the seed to which I have referred. If this House is in sympathy with the proposals to this effect which have been advanced from time to time by different boards of trade and by different municipal councils throughout the country, I feel satisfied that the request will be granted and this motion allowed to go into effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The matter of production is, of course, a very important one, and within the next few days I shall be glad to look into the subject of my hon. friend's motion and see what, if anything, can be done. I spoke to my hon. friend the other day, and I understood that it was not his intention to bring this resolution up until after the Budget. I do not understand that he is pressing the motion to-day, and if he is content to withdraw it, having brought it to the attention of the Government, I shall be very glad to look into the matter.

I have no desire to press the matter against the wishes of the Minister of Finance, but if it is some time before the Budget is brought down and the people do not know what course the Government purposes adopting, the result may be detrimental to the best interests of this year's crop. It will be satisfactory, however, if the farmers have the seed before May 24 or June 1. Undoubtedly they are anxious to know whether the Government will grant

this request, for if the duty he removed many farmers will put in seed who otherwise would, perhaps, be unable to secure the necessary seed or who would not be anxious _to pay the price which they have to pay under existing, circumstances.
As I should like to say a few words on this resolution, I would move that the debate be now adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I agree to that.
Motion agreed to, and debate adjourned.

Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Rouville) moved for:
A copy of the Order in Council increasing the toll rates on Victoria Bridge, Montreal, and also a copy of all petitions, telegrams, letters and other documents referring to said increase.
[Mr. McCoig.j
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any length. .1 wish only to draw the attention of the Government to the very serious state of affairs which exists in connection with the toll rates on Victoria bridge, Montreal, which is the only connecting link across the river St. Lawrence between the great commercial metropolis of Canada and the south shore. A few weeks ago the people were startled to learn that the toll rates were increased. I do not know the reason for the change, but I wish to inform my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways and Canals, that some relief should certainly be afforded to. the farmers of the counties on the south shore. I have not the present tariff before me, but I know the rates are simply prohibitive for the farmers of the counties of Laprairie, Rouville, Chambly and Vercheres, not to mention others, and I sincerely hope that the representatives of the pi ovince of Quebec in the Government will do something to remove that disability which is fastened upon the farmers of the south shore. The increase, I am sure, has passed unnoticed when my hon. friends were absent from Council, but it seems to me that to call their attention to this real grievance will be sufficient to effect a cure.
I think the time has come when the Grand Trunk Railway Company should give us free ingress and free egress across the Victoria bridge. This bridge has been very heavily subsidized, first for the original construction and later on for its reconstruction, so that it seems to me that the people in that section of the country should receive ample justice on the part of that company. I quite understand that, like all other transportation companies, the Grand Trunk Railway has passed through hard times; but when one considers that such a large population has to make use of that connecting link between the two shores of the St. Lawrence river, one feels that the Government should make it a point, if not to make the bridge free for the farmers and the community at large, at least to have the old toll rates restored. I make a special appeal to the hon. Secretary of State, (Mr. Paten-aude), who represents one of the large constituencies of the city of Montreal, and also to the Deputy Speaker of the House (Mr. Rainville) who represents the counties of Chambly and Vercheres.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend must be mistaken, because there has been no change in the rates so far as the farmers are concerned; the change is only as re-

gards motor trucks, and I presume the Minister of Railways will have an explanation for that. *

Perhaps I should reply to
the hon. member, as this matter was brought before me when I was acting for the Minister of Railways in his absence. The matter is one of routine. After having heard the case as represented by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, [DOT] I went into it thoroughly with the deputy minister and other officials, and found that the tolls had not been revised for many years. The deputy minister, after investigating the matter very carefully, recommended that the changes were fair and just, and I therefore recommended the changes to Council and they were approved. The changes, however, were not so drastic as the hon. member has stated. At the time care was taken to protect the farmers and the increase was more in regard to motor trucks. After the Order in Council was passed, I noticed that there were some complaints, but I understand they were taken up with the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and that the grievances complained of were removed. At all events I gave notice to the effect that if there were any grievances,
4 p.m. these toll rates could be revised from time to time, and I was willing at any time to hear complaints which, if well founded, would result in a revision of the rates. From that day, however, -to the time that I ceased administering the department, no complaint was registered. I have- not asked the minister if any complaints have been received since then, but I have been advised by the Grand Trunk officials themselves and others that there are no grievances now, or that if there are any, they are so small that no one cares to take any further interest in them. As my hon. friend knows, the matter can be brought before the Minister of Railways at any time, and I am quite satisfied that he will do his best to remedy any grievance that is shown to exist. The rates are not permanent; they can be revised at any time.

I am very glad to hear that the rates can be revised when a grievance is shown to exist. In the present case the grievance is certainly felt by the farmers, and also by the business men of Montreal. My hon. friend, (Mr. Patenaude) stated that the farmers were not hit by this new regulation. Well, I can say this:
I represent the constituency of Rouville,
which, as my hon. friend knows, is a farming community, and when I was there ten or twelve days ago I met several farmers both of St. Hyacinthe and Rouville, and the whole talk was of the rates on the Victoria Bridge. My hon. friend must not forget that motor trucks are used very extensively in that very progressive district, in the Counties of Laprarie, Rouville, and Chambly-Vercheres. I need not say that it is the most progressive district in my province. I have also heard some very bitter complaints from the merchants of Montreal. I am sure my hon. friend will bear me out when I say that there is a large local trade between Montreal and the south sllhore. The wholesale grocers of Montreal send motor trucks over the Victoria Bridge, simply loaded with merchandise to be delivered at Laprairie, St. Lambert, Chambly, Longueuil, Marieville, and other smaller towns and villages. I have heard some members of the Montreal Board of Trade complain very bitterly about these high rates, and I might mention many who do an extensive business on the south shore. They stated that the rates were almost prohibitive. I am glad to have had this ppportunity of bringing the matter before the House, and to have the promise of the acting minister that a remedy 'will be found for this evil.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. RODOLPHE LEMIEUX (Rouville) moved for:
A copy of all letters, telegrams, petitions and all other papers concerning- the substitution of the name of Luceville given to the Intercolonial Railway station of Sainte Luce, County of Rimousld, Quebec.
He said: This motion will be more interesting to those members of the House who are familiar with the French language. Sainte Luce, the old name of the village is a much better name than Luceville. It was an old French name and was euphonious. Sombody, possibly a busybody in the village, undertook to get the name of the post office and station changed, and against the will of the parish priest and of the community generally, and in spite of shoals of protesting letters and telegrams, the name was changed to Luceville. This is really a grievance for that constituency, not only to those who appreciate euphony and like to stick to old names with a romance about them, but from a business point of view as well. I sincerely hope that my hon. friend the Secretary of State, who attends to our

affairs in the province of Quebec, will see to it that the old name of Sainte Luce is restored. Some people in the Province of Quebec have a very officious way of getting old names with a flavour of romance about them changed for new names which have no meaning at all. What meaning has Luceville? It is ugly, it is not euphonious, and there is no romance about it; whereas the old name of Sainte Luce has a pleasant ring about it. I sincerely trust that my hon. friend will see that the name of the station and of the post office is restored.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. B. McCOIG (West Kent) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, on account of the urgent need of greater production of foodstuffs and the admitted shortage of farm labour, tractor engines suitable for all kinds of farm work, which will be of great assistance to producers, should be admitted into Canada free of duty.
He said: I feel satisfied that every member of the House will agree with me that it is of supreme importance that this resolution should be passed. We have it on the highest authority that there is great food shortage at this time. The Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) and the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) have urged our farmers to produce as much as possible. But, with the great shortage of labour, especially in the province of Ontario, it is out of the question for our farmers, under present conditions, to get in the crops that our people are anxious they should get in. I was talking to Mr. Foulds, manager of the Thames Valley Land Company, which has large holdings in the township of Tilbury, in the county of Kent, and he informed me that fields aggregating no less than four hundred acres in the most fertile portion of their lands would be left uncultivated this year owing to the shortage of labour and the lateness of the season. I asked him whether, if he had a light tractor engine, he would be able to handle the entire farm, and his answer was that he believed he could. He said he had been communicating with the''provincial authorities with a view to getting one of the ten tractors purchased by the Government of the province. But it is likely he would be unsuccessful because of the great demand 	-
that has arisen for these tractors. It goes to show how urgently the tractors are needed when Ithe provincial Government purchases ten of them and brings them from the other side of the line, where they are manufactured. We learn, also, that the -enterprising members of the Board of Trade of Toronto are drawing upon their private bank accounts to purchase five tractors with a view to distributing them where they can do the best work. With such evidences of an urgent demand for these machines on the part of our own people, it would seem only fair that this Parliament should take action at least to the extent of allowing these tractors to be brought in without an additional fine. I believe that if the duty were removed many farmers would be able to purchase these tractors privately, and if the duty were removed the cost to the purchasers would be greatly reduced. The tariff formerly was 20 per cent and now there is an additional 7i per cent. That is to say, if this duty were taken off we should be able to purchase five tractors for the present cost of four. I believe I am within the mark when I say that at present one thousand of these tractors could be used in Ontario. If the duty were removed these machines would be of some assistance in getting in -the spring crop, and our farmers would be in a much better position to put in an additional wheat crop this fall, and in the meantime there would be the summer fallowing and preparation for that crop. I understand from newspaper reports that other countries have placed orders for no fewer than 50,000 farm tractors.
' This is an indication of how widely useful these machines can be made in assisting greater agricultural production, and makes all the stronger the case in favour of this resolution. ' Should the Government object to allowing the free entry of the larger tractors, I would be prepared to amend this resolution by confining it to tractors of 8-16 horse-power, or possibly 10-20 horsepower. That, I understand to mean, a tractor that will pull 8 or 10 horse-power and will develop power on the belt of 16 or 20 horse-power. These tractors will be sufficiently large for our immediate purposes, and their importation will not interfere with any manufacture in Canada. I believe that the Massey-Harris Company are getting out a small tractor, but it is practically still in the experimental stage. We see by the press this morning that in all churches throughout the Dominion preachers have been urging greater production. And we

are warned by those who are in a better position to judge than most of the members of this House can possibly be that there is danger in the Old .World, and even here, of actual famine. This being so, it is clearly the duty of Parliament to give farmers every possible assistance. With the use of these tractors our farmers will be able to produce more, and thus Canada, besides sending her men to the front, will be able to give assistance in providing supplies for the troops and the people generally without which we cannot succeed in winning the war.
Sir THOMAS WHITE (Minister of Finance! : I am not clear as to what item in the Tariff the hon. member refers to. The resolution speaks of "tractor engines suitable for all kinds of farm work." These engines to-day are manufactured in Canada, by one or more concerns. Some time ago we placed ditching machines on the free list, but that was partly on the ground that they were not manufactured in Canada. As I have pointed out in the House before, one item in the Tariff depends upon another. If we take away the duty on tractor engines, then, as tractor engines are manufactured in Canada, we should have to take away the duties on the raw materials which enter into their manufacture, on the coal used in their production, and even on the building material used in the construction of the buildings in which they are produced.
Will the minister please say where these tractor engines are manufactured in Canadia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Assuming that I understand the -article to which he refers, I am informed that they are manufactured in Hamilton, Brantford, and possibly some other places.
I may inform -the minister that the 8-10, and 10-20 tractors are not manufactured in Canada, though I understand that the Massey-Harris people are experimenting with them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: But the nation wilfstarve in the meantime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do nob agree
that these machines cannot be made in Canada. My information is that they are actually manufactured here and can be bought. It is the policy of the Government to encourage the manufacture of all articles that can he produced in Canada. It is in the national interest now more *than ever that if an article can toe bought in Canada it should be bought here rather than abroad, for it is necessary above all in time ,of war that we should conserve our resources. Speaking also from the standpoint of revenue, there never was a time when this Dominion needed revenue more than it does at present.
Import the goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There never was a time when this Dominion needed revenue more than it does at present. Our war expenditures are at the rate of $1,000,000 a day.
Mr. PUG8LEY: Some time ago I eaw in the newspapers that the British Government had bought, for -the use of its farmers, 2,000 of these tractor ploughs. I suppose that is what my hon. friend (Mr. McCoig) means. Were any of these purchased in Canada or were they not all purchased in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information as ta that point, but I-am perfectly [DOT]satisfied that if the Dominion Government desired to buy 2,000 ploughs it would be very much better that they should place the order for them in the Dominion of Canada than in the United States.
If you could get them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the point is that while we might get these tractors in the United States, they are manufactured, or can he manufactured, in Canada and in ordinary times it is desirable that our Canadian manufacturers should build them.
Does the hon. gentleman say they can be bought in Canada? I understand the Ontario Government are bringing them in from the United States. Why are they doing that if they can buy them here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not able to say whether the Ontario Government are buying them in the United States or not, but I am referring to traction engines. Traction engines are manufactured in Canada.

I think it will clear matters up a little bit if we get an idea Of the kind of engine that is meant. You can get a traction engine to run a threshing'machine in Canada; they are made at half a dozen or a dozen places. But, the tractor engines that are now being used by the western farmers for drawing a double mould board, or a two or four furrow plough, are not made in Canada except experimentally. We cannot get them in quantity; we have to buy them in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will observe the wording of the resolution. It refers to "tractor engines suitable for all kinds of farm work."

I suggested when I was
making my remarks that I would be willing to so amend my resolution as to confine it to the 8-16 and 10-20 tractors which are suitable for farm purposes. The large tractor-s, the 20-30 and 20-40, are too heavy for farm work and are almost impracticable' because they pack the ground too much.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not possible for me to agree to the amendment of this motion unless my hon. friend desires to give notice of it. I can only speak of the resolution as it. stands on the Order Paper, and as it stands on the Order Paper it should be voted down for the reason which I have given; that is, that -the tractor engines can be manufactured in Canada, and it is against the national interest that they should be imported from the United States. I was developing my argument as to the need that Canada has for additional revenue. Then, beyond the desirability of manufacturing these goods in Canada, if there ever was a time in the history of the Dominion when we need revenue it is the present. We have an expenditure in connection with this war at the rate of $1,000,000 a day. In so far as I know, all classes in the community are doing well. I do not think that the farmers have ever done as well in the history of the Dominion as they are doing at the present time. I do not believe that as high prices have ever been obtained for farm produce as are being obtained at present. I do not believe that general business in the Dominion was ever better or as good as it is at the present time. That being so, there would seem to be no tMr. Pardee.]
reason why the' duty should be taken off these articles any more than off a further range of articles that my hon. friend might mention. The present is not a time to reduce or remove duties which give us our revenue. So that, on two grounds, first, on the ground of revenue, second, on the ground that these articles are being, or can be, manufactured in Canada, I think my hon. gentleman's motion should be negatived. If he desires to withdraw this motion and substitute a motion which covers a certain line of traction engines which he mentioned, but which I cannot identify and about which I have no information at the present time, I would be willing that that should be done, but, as it stands, the resolution should be negatived.

Mr. Speaker, I want, in the first place, to associate myself with those who are in favour of any measure that will benefit the agricultural classes of this country at this time. I am rather inclined to the view, however, that the suggestion which has been made by my hon. friend from West Kent (Mr. McCoig) this afternoon, if carried into effect, would not be the benefit to the farmers that he anticipates, but would, on the other hand, work a great injury. We have in the little town of Essex, six miles from where I live, a splendid industry which is branching out into the manufacture of farm tractors. They are putting up at the present time, I understand, seven of these tractors for the express purpose of assisting in all light farm work. If my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) were to act upon the suggestion of my hon. friend from West Kent, I think it would have the effect of wiping out of existence that infant industry, which, I do believe, is [DOT] contrary to the policy of both political parties. As I understand the principle upon which both political parties stand in regard to this matter, it is that the infant industry shall have a reasonable protection until such time as it is enabled to compete against the industries of the outside world. My hon. friend (Mr. McCoig) says that is false. There may be some question about that point, but I know that up our way in the splendid city of Windsor, where we are hoping to build up a great industrial centre, the Liberals have very little to say about free trade.
The hon. gentleman did not say what you intimated at all.

I did, not address any
remarks to the hon. gentleman whatever.

I did not refer in any way whatever to anything that the hon. gentleman said. That is all imaginary on the part of the hon. gentleman.

I heard a breath floating from the other side that sounded like that. I may be pardoned for referring to the question of traction ditchers which has been dealt with. I think the Minister of Finance will agree when I state that I was the first member of this House who suggested to him that, as this machine was not manufactured in Canada and was only manufactured in the United States, it might be placed on the free list. I have watched this very closely because the question of tile draining in the county of Essex and in western Ontario, where it is a flat, level, but very rich and fertile country, is a live issue and we have dozens of these machines in our neighborhood. There is one working on my own farm, or on my father's farm, and we know, what we had to pay when these machines had a duty imposed upon them. We had to pay twenty-five cents a rod for the digging of the*trench and the placing of the tile. .The duty was taken off. A few more- machines were brought in and the men who brought the machines in joined together and raised the cost of laying the tile to twenty-eight cents a rod. That is what we are paying to-day. So that the elimination of the duty on the tile ditching machines did not reduce the price to the farmer of the laying of the tile, but, in my opinion, it did have the effect for all time to come, while the tariff remains as it is, of preventing all possibility of any tile ditching machines being constructed in the Dominion of Canada. So it seems to me that when our policy is based upon that principle of a reasonable protection for an infant industry, when we are commencing to build up that industry, I believe, as the ' farmers of this country have been loyal and patriotic in their adherence to that principle in our national policy in the past, they will stand by it in the future in the same way. I also believe that the benefit which my hon. friend anticipates would flow from the reduction of duty would not be secured. Therefore, I think the tariff should remain as it is.
What firm in Essex are making' these machines?

The firm there is making a farm tractor with a capacity of drawing two or three plows. They have purchased a machine shop and commenced operations
about two months ago. I am quite confident that if my hon. friend will sendN a telegram this afternoon, that company will be able to fill right away all the orders that he can take in the county of Kent.

Last fall-I did not want to bring any personal matter into this debate-I waited on Mr. McGregor, head of the Ford factory in Ford, and asked when I could get a tractor for my own farm, as at the request of this Government I wanted one to get in all the wheat possible. Mr. McGregor told me that he could not guarantee me a tractor within two years; and the whole nation would starve before these tractors would be ready to cultivate land to produce wheat.

If the hon. member will
wire to the Canadian Engine Company at Dunnville, Ontario, he can get a tractor because we manufacture them.
What horse-power?
I do not know exactly the horse-power, but large enough to do ploughing.	.
That is the trouble, they are too large.
These are kerosene burning engines and they afford a great saving in cost over the gasolene engines to which my hon. friend (Mr. Lalor) referred.

Are the McGregor people at Ford the same as the firm at Essex?
Mr. tyiLCOX: No, they are not the same people. The Ford people have not commenced to construct tractors. I understand they have not commenced even in Detroit, and I know they have not in Walkerville. The firm I have reference to is starting a factory in the town of Essex.
What is the name of the firm?
I think it is The Essex County Tractor Company, but I would not be positive as to the name.
Have they produced these tractors yet?
I shall send a telegram this afternoon and get that information. I am sure they are now manufacturing tractors and putting them on the market. They had one on exhibition at the fall fair last year.

The reason I ask these questions is that I wish to be absolutely

fair in these things. So far as the Ford people are concerned, I know that what the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) says is correct, because I wrote them myself and they are not in a position to produce any tractors yet. As to the factory in Essex, I never heard of it before. That of course, does not say, that it does not exist. I wish them success. But in the meantime I want to impress on the Minister of Finance that this year in Ontario we are suffering very materially from the lack of farm labour. There is a great deal in the newspapers about the city people sending students into the country and going themselves, and all that sort of thing; but as a matter of fact the ordinary farmer does not pay much attention to that because he knows as well as I do that a man cannot [DOT] come from the city, unaccustomed to heavy manual labour, and be much use on the farm.
Men from the city have proved to be good fighters and I do not know why they should not be good farmers if they apply themselves.

They would undoubtedly become good farmers if they had the time and experience, as good as anybody else. But at the same time no man can successfully do a kind of work to which he is not accustomed until he has had training and experience. The tractors of which the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) speaks were exhibited last year at all the ploughing matches in the country. They were all of American manufacture. The tariff at the present time as against American machines is 20 per cent and 71 per .cent, or-27i per cent. The machines that [DOT] were exhibited and were .put into use last fall, -these American machines, were very light and capable, with engines able to draw two or three ploughs. I saw them working in two or three instances and know that they did excellent work and could be used on the ordinary farm at least in central and western Ontario. I think it would be a material advantage to the people of Ontario, and, perhaps, to other parts of the country if this change in the tariff were made. I leave my hon. friends to speak for the West, but it would certainly be of material advantage to us if the duty were taken off. A duty of 271 per cent is very high; if is altogether unnecessarily high. I do not know of any manufacture that requires a duty of 271 per cent to do business in this country. The minister is quite right in saying that if an article is manufactured in Canada
[iMr. Nesbitt.]
and the duty is taken off the finished article the duty should also he removed from the raw material entering into its production. But for the benefit of the farmer and of the community at large, it would be wise for the minister to remove the duty from light tractors used for ploughing purposes, and I hope he will give this matter serious consideration. I am sure that the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) will be willing to -amend his resolution to conform to that suggestion.

It seems to me that when so -much -has been said by the Government in connection with greater production, this matter deserves serious consideration. A campaign is being carried on all over Canada to-day, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, calling on the farmers to produce more foodstuffs, and there is absolutely no question that the world's supply of food is now at a lower ebb than it has been for many, many years. It was stated last week by an authority engaged in compiling figures relating to this matter that during the present year the amount of wheat produced will be 310,000,000 bushels less than the different countries that use wheat as a food have been in the habit of importing yearly. In view of this shortage and of the necessity for all the production possible, it would seem to be a matter of common sense on the part of the Finance Minister and of the Government to help along production by granting the request made by the member for Kent. There is no use preaching production to a farmer if the conditions are not such that he can produce with advantage to himself. If you want to secure the greatest possible amount of production, the proper course is to make the way easy for the man who produces.
I am quite sure -that the tractors that the member for Kent wishes to have put on the free list are quite different from the ones that -the Minister of Finance spoke about. The traction engines that we have seen in the West by the hundreds are engines that can be used for a number of purposes, chiefly for running separators; they move from field to field by their own power and draw the separator and a wagon or two along with them. That is not the sort of engine that the member for Kent wants to have put on the free list. The engine to which he refers takes the place of six or eight horses. Hundreds of them are being used in the provinces of Mani-

toba, Saskatchewan and Alberta; they will do as much breaking as eight or nine horses. I know- one firm in Winnipeg which has made a contract with a Minneapolis manufacturer for the purchase of several hundred of these tractors; they are being bought throughout the whole country. They retail at a rather high price, something like $1,650; but in the West they find that a tractor of that kind, notwithstanding the high cost of fuel oil, does the work cheaper and more quickly than it can be done by using horses, especially in breaking up the land. A number of these tractors, all from the United States, were exhibited at exhibitions last summer. I think I can reasonably assure the Finance Minister that the tractor engine referred to by the member for Kent is not manufactured for practical puposes in Canada. I believe, however that the manufacturers are taking the matter up, and it is probable that in a year or two they will Have an engine on the market that will be all right. If these tractors were being manufactured in Canada, I feel certain that the Government of Ontario would have purchased them from Canadian manufacturers instead of going to the United States for them. The fact that they bought them in the United States is conclusive proof that they could not secure them in the province of Ontario.
If the duty upon these tractors were removed, one result would be. a very much increased crop during the year 1918. I dp not know that the removal of the duty would make much difference so far as the present year's crop is concerned. In another month the sowing season will be over, and those who have not obtained tractors would haTdly be able to secure them in time to use them advantageously between now and the end of the seeding. We have no certainty that the war will 'be over a year from now, but we do know that food is becoming very much scarcer in Britain. I see that the British Government have arranged with Mr. Henry Ford, the maker of the Ford automobile, to send specifications of his tractor engine to Britain. The British Government will then have these tractors manufactured in Great Britain -and used to plough up the parks and vacant lots throughout the British Isles in order to secure the cultivation of a largely increased acreage. If it is necessary for the British Government to take such drastic steps as these in order to increase their own food supply, it seems to
me that it would be wise for this Parliament to do everything in its power to increase the supply of wheat, not only this year, but during next year as well. From all the information I have been able to get in the West, I understand that the acreage in wheat this year will be less than last year, on account of last fall being a bad season. Only a small amount of land was got ready for this spring, and while the total acreage in crop this year w-ill not be less than last year, the acreage in wheat will be considerably less, that of flax, barley and oats being, perhaps, somewhat larger. We have to take it for granted that there will be a big demand for food next year, and it is not wise to wait until next year to prepare for the sowing of the 1918 crop. We have to begin to prepare now, and we can do no better than adopt the resolution of the member for Kent and have these tractors put on the free list. The wording of the resolution is, perhaps a little wide; it might be better to narrow it down and state more definitely just what kind of tractor is meant. If my hon. friend the member fox Kent and the Minister pf Finance get together, they can very soon arrange that.
I s-ay again that if the Government wish to carry out the policy of more production they ought to adopt the suggestion made by the member for Kent and put these tractors on the free list. It would be a big help to the farmers not only of Ontario, but of the three prairie provinces a-s well, and the result would be a largely increased acreage during the season of 1018.

Mr. G. E. McCRANEY (Saskatoon) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: As the Railway Act is under revision by a Special Committee of the House, this appears an opportune time to bring to the consideration of the House and of this committee the amendment proposed by this Bill. The purpose is to give to the members of the local Legislatures similar pass privileges to those enjoyed by members of this Parliament. It is not proposed to add any new burden to the railway companies, for it is the practice of railway companies to give passes to the members of the provincial legislatures. It may be of interest to the House to know under what circumstances section 343 of the Railway Act, which it is here proposed to amend, was passed. I am informed that in 1903' the late Senator Davis of Prince Albert, being then a member of this House, made some criticism of one of the railway companies, from which company he held a pass. The criticism was objectionable to the company, and they promptly withdrew the pass and so notified Mr. Davis. He spoke to the late Mr. Blair, who was then Minister of Railways, telling him of the circumstance. As the Railway Act was then under the consideration of Parliament, this section was put in so as to avoid the recurrence of such instances and to place members of Parliament on an independent footing with reference to the railways. This subject of passes has been and is a matter of discussion on public platforms. The fact that a member of the legislature holds a pass from a railway company beoomes the subject of remark. To my mind, members of provincial legislatures are entitled to the same protection for their personal honour that members of this House are entitled to. The legislature of Nova Scotia lias, endeavoured to deal with the matter. In the Statutes of Nova Scotia, 1906, Chapter 25, section 3, the following is enacted:
234a. Every railway company shall furnish free transportation upon any of its trains for members of the Legislative Council and House of Assembly of Nova Scotia, with their baggage, and also for such officers and servants as may be employed by the Governor in Council in business or work connected with the railways of the province, or any of them, with their baggage or equipment, and shall also when required haul free of charge any car provided for the Governor-in-Council.
Whether the legislature of the province of Nova Scotia has the power to pass such an Act affecting railways under the control of this Parliament is a matter I am not going to discuss. But I understand that the practice of the railways .is to conform to

this section and to issue passes to members of the legislature. The legislature has done all it could, at any rate, to put its members in a Tight light before the country. I am informed by leaders of the Opposition in two of the provinces that the passes which are issued to them by the railway companies cover transportation, not only within the province in which they reside, but also over the whole of their system. Perhaps when the matter is under consideration, it may be desirable to give them the same privileges which it is proposed by this Bill to give to members of Provincial Cabinets. The Bill, as it is presented, limits the passes of members of the' legislature to transportation within the province in which they reside, while providing for passes to be given to members of Provincial Cabinets good throughout the whole of Canada.

I cannot altogether agree with this Bill, and I would suggest that it be referred to the Committee on Railways without giving it the second reading. I think it is going rather further than we should go to compel railways to give transportation to all members of provincial legislatures. I understood the hon. member (Mr. McCraney) to say that the railways gave to members of the Nova Scotia legislature passes that are good over their entire systems. That is not the case so far as the. Government railways are concerned. I think that on company railways also such passes are confined to the limits of the province except in the case of the ministers of the Crown.

The minister is correct-members of the legislature are given transportation within the province in which they reside, hut ministers of the Grown have passes good throughout the whole system. That is what-this Bill provides.

I was endeavouring to get the
full import of the views exx ressed by my bon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley). I think I succeeded to the extent of learning the principle upon which he understands the present enactment was inserted in the Railway Act, namely, that if being in the public interest- that members of thife House should be enabled to ascertain to *the very best advantage the conditions. in all parts of -Canada, it was well that they should be free at all times to travel in the different parts of the country and that they 'should be free to do so * under -such legislation as would make it their right and not make it an obligation on their part to the railway companies. I do not purpose to argue it now. It might be that the logical extension of that principle would be to enable members o-f the provincial legislatures to travel within the borders of their provinces. But I cannot for the life of me understand how, by -any extension of the principle we adopted in this House -some years ago, it could be argued that that right should be extended to members of provincial legislatures to travel throughout

the length and breadth of Canada. Whether, if this Act go no further than to enable members of the provincial legislatures to travel within the borders of their own province, it would then be acceptable, I would not care to say.

That is as far as it
does go.

It appears to me that as a general principle the shorter our steps, and the less distance we go in that direction the better. Every one knows the abuses to which these rights, or alleged rights, are always put. But, at all events, the proposal, in its present form, does not appear to be one which should be adopted in principle, if the passage of the second reading would mean adoption in principle, because it goes further in my judgment than we can justify ourselves in going.

As I read the Bill it is limited to the provinces. It says:
and to members of the Executive Councils of the provinces of Canada, and within the provinces in which they reside, to members of the Legislative Councils and Legislative Assemblies of the provinces of Canada.
Except as to members of the Government, it is limited to the province; as to members of the Government it is broader.

I do not see the signifi canee of the conjunction in that event or even that it meets the objection that could be raised to the principle. At all events, I should not care to concede or extend the right further without the fullest consideration. I would suggest that, without adopting the principle of the Bill, it be referred to the committee to which all 1 railway amendments are now referred.
That means, as I understand, the -second reading without affirming the principle?
Yes.
Alotion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and referred to the Committee on Railways.
I rather thought the Solicitor General meant-and I think that is what the Minister of Railways would do-to refer this to the special committee.
No, to the Railway Committee of the House.

I understand from the Solicitor General that it was a special com-

mittee to which he thought this Bill should be referred and not to the general Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines. I moved the motion on the understanding that all amendments are being considered-now by this special committee on railway matters, and I see by the public press that the Minister of Railways is inviting suggestions by letter and otherwise. That is the committee which should consider this Bill.

I have no objection to telling you why, bub in the absence of the person who 'is directly interested, I am reluctant to say anything concerning this matter. I do not like to speak disparagingly of one who has no opportunity of saying anything by way of explanation, or defen-ce, or mitigation. I suppose it is so in all cases where the person concerned is not a member of this House; whatever you have to say touching a matter of this kind has to be said in his absence, and he, therefore, has no opportunity of saying anything by way of explanation. I would like to know why.

The immediate cause of his suspension arose in this way: on a Saturday evening in the latter part of February he applied to the deputy minister for leave of absence for a few days. As the matter of his absence had been up at least on one occasion before, the deputy referred him to me. Mr. Brown telephoned me to say his wife was leaving the city on Monday and that he would like to have three or four days off. I said, "all right; take three or four days." Well, he took all that week and three days of the next week, and when he returned he did not say anything about it, make any explanation, apology, or anything else. I, therefore, gave him notice of suspension. The facts are that for a long time he had not been satisfactorily discharging the duties of his office. He appeared to be obsessed with a grossly exaggerated conception of the importance of a civil servant in the first division. He used to do things without saying anything about them, a thing which I think a man in his position should not have done. He used to do things that he was distinctly told not to do, and he would criticise the way in which the Department of Labour was administered.
He was justified in that.	-

The department may
not be managed properly; it may be very inefficiently administered; but it appeared to me it was no part of the duty of an assistant deputy minister to criticise the way in which the department was administered. I do not think he was competent to discharge the duties of his office; I think he was incompetent; I think he was insubordinate, and he was disloyal.
In what sense was he disloyal?
In the sense that he was not loyal to the head of the department.

I suppose the same
thing will apply in any of the other departments, that if an employee asks leave of absence for a certain length of time, and stays away three or four or five times longer than he is permitted, he will be suspended?

I do not know what
action the other ministers would take in a case of that kind.

I am not asking the
minister to tell me whether that course of action will apply or not; but I say for the benefit of the other ministers that there are men employed in the other departments who have asked for leave of absence for a very short space of time who have travelled all through the West for four or five months.

I have not had very much experience in any other department; but I have acted in a few of the other departments in the absence of the ministers, and I remember distinctly deputies coming in and apologizing for being away half a day, and giving reasons for their absence; such as sickness in the family or something of that sort, and, of course,, nothing more was said about the matter. In this case, however, no effort at all was made to explain or apologize.
It was not a question of apology; it was a question of whether or not he was competent to fill the position.
I gave incompetency as one reason; there are several others.

Apparently the reason given is that this official took two or three days longer leave of absence than he had asked for, and because on his return he did not come to the minister and apologize, the minister first suspended him and then fired him, and now the minister brings in

a further excuse that the official was not competent anyway. If the assistant deputy minister was not competent, it has taken the minister five years to find that out. He was not suspended or dismissed for incompetency; but simply because he did not apologize to the minister for being two or three days over his leave he was fired.

I do not know whether my hon. friend knows better than I why he was fired. I have told the committee why his services were dispensed with. My hon. friend is probably right, that his services should have been dispensed with five years ago; 1 know that I spoke about it several years ago. I may add that he has not received any statutory increase of salary for three or four years because he had pot, in my judgment, efficiently discharged the duties of his .office.

The minister should tell us in what respect Mr. Brown was incompetent and also in what particular respect he was disloyal. I know nothing about Mr. Brown except that he was always regarded by the public as an efficient officer; but if a man is said by a minister of the Crown to be incompetent and disloyal, those general words ought to be particularized, and definite instances given in which the incompetency has arisen and the disloyalty become apparent. It is very easy to use those words in a general sense and

they carry meanings which are very broad. Mr. Brown is a journalist; I remember when he was in the press gallery here, and while he was in the department, as far as competency is concerned, his intelligence and capacity ought to have made him competent for the office. Therefore, if the minister says he is incompetent, I ask: Wherein is he incompetent? The same applies to the question of his disloyalty. It is only fair that we should know these things.

As my hon. friend from Pictou has said, when Mr. Brown was appointed to a position in the Department of Labour, he had been a newspaper reporter of some experience, but no distinction. He was appointed to the position without any examination whatever, under the provisions of section 21 of the Civil Service Amendment Act, the Civil Service Commission after profound deliberation for three months gravely certified that the duties of this office called for qualifications of a professional and technical character. As hon. gentlemen will remember, under section 21 of the Civil Service Amendment Act, a man may be appointed without any examination whatever when it is certified by the Civil Service Commission that the duties of the office call for qualifications of a professional, technical or otherwise peculiar character, and in this case such a certificate was given. If a university graduate were to apply for a position carrying a salary of $500 a year, he or she would have to pass an examination; but under this certificate, issued by the Civil Service Commission in this case, this man was ap- , pointed at a salary of $2,800 a year to ad- ' vance to $4,000 by annual increments of $100. That- is a little device that is sometimes adopted to foist into the service one who cannot get in by the regular route.

I think the present Government knows more about that than anybody else.
Mr.^ CROTHERS: I do not think you will find any men of that kind in the Labour Department.
' Mr. GRAHAM: I guess the other ministers are pretty bad, then.

I remember on one occasion he went down

What practical -steps has the minister taken ito deal with the problem of the high cost of living in Canada? I am aware that an Order in Council was passed in regard to the matter, and that Mr. O'Qonnor has been employed in that connection, but so far I have been unable to observe that in any part of Canada the Government have taken hold of this problem with any strength or vigour or in such way as to produce results. In Australia, where they have a War Measures Act similar to ours, the Government have taken vast powers and have regulated the cost of staple products which enter into the daily, life of the citizens of the country. We have had nothing of that kind here, and I think the minister ought to tell us what he has tried t<? do, even though he has not succeeded in doing very much, to meet the paramount necessity which exists all over Canada, particularly among the labouring people, of dealing with the exorbitant cost of all the necessaries of life.

I have a Teport in
process of preparation, which will be ready in a few days, and which will go into particulars concerning the matter to which
my hon. friend directs attention. However, I do not mind telling him, in a general way, what we have done. The Order in Council, a copy of which I have not at hand, is aimed at preventing restriction of trade, exorbitant prices, combines, and so on. For instance, it makes it obligatory for one who is in possession of articles of food, clothing or fuel-the Order in Council is confined to these three classes of goods-in amounts more than ordinarily necessary for his own use or for carrying on his business, to sell these goods at a fair and reasonable price. We took up the question of coal. We sent to every known coal dealer in Canada a number of questions which were very full and very searching. He was required to say where he bought the coal in the first place, what he paid for it at point of shipment, what the freight cost him, the cost of unloading and selling, and the amount of his overhead expenses. Satisfactory sworn, returns were obtained town nearly all the coal dealers in Canada. It was necessary in some cases to communicate with the firms more than once, hut in the end I think we got answers to all the questions which were asked. With one or two exceptions we were satisfied that no unreasonable profits were made foy the retail dealers in coal. We got statements of prices, and .so on, not only from them, but from other sources as well, and were enabled to compare the two, and with the exception of one place, I do not remember that any complaints were made that the people were being overcharged for their coal. Then we took up the price of sugar. We found that an agreement existed between the manufacturers and wholesale and retail men with regard to prices.	.
After some correspondence, some of these men came to see us, and in many cases, if not in all of them, the practice which we thought objectionable was discontinued. I know one refinery, for instance, that controlled the sale of sugar in two provinces, and only fifty-two men in the two provinces could buy sugar from that refinery, no one being able to purchase sugar from it unless he belonged to the association or complied with the conditions necessary to become a member of the association. We took the matter up; the attorneys general of the provinces consented that a prosecution should be taken against those men, the result being that they came down from their perch and discontinued this objectionable practice. We have investigated the cold

storage business throughout the country; we have examined into the way in which collieries are conducted as to prices and all that sort of thing, and in a few days I will have ready a full report which I expect to placed upon the Table and which will set forth the details of what we have done in these various lines. Of course, the great majority of the people of this country understand the main factors in the rise of prices, although they are confidently told by those who have an object in view that there are other causes. It is probably safe to say that thirty million men, if not a good many more, have been withdrawn from productive work to engage in destructive work. It is said that those men consume at least fifty per cent more than they would if they were civilians. That gives us the equivalent of 45,000,000 men consuming foodstuffs and producing nothing, withdrawn from productive labour and engaged in destructive labour. Before the war broke out, there was just about enough food grown to cover the world's consumption; we had not to throw any surplus food into the ocean. Take 45,000,000 men from producing; set them to destroy life and property; take that, in connection with the fact that last year, with slight exceptions in certain places, crops were short the world over, and with all this destruction and waste going on lessening production, and you have the main factors causing the advance in prices. Some people tell us that the rise in prices is due to cold storage and combinations. I admit that in some cases those things have had a slight influence on prices, but the main factors are those I have stated. We are endeavouring under that Order in Council to offset so far as we can those influences that, to a slight extent, may affect prices, but on the whole the others are the.' main factors.	,

With regard to ships, I say that this Government, so far as the question of transportation is concerned, have absolutely fallen down in the discharge of their 10 p.m. duty. This war has been in progress since August, 1914, well on to three years. Surely this Government ought to have recognized that the result of the great European war would be a greater demand for vessels. They ought to have realized that there would be-the submarine warfare, that the shipping of Great Britain and her Allies would be imperilled and that there would so be a greater demand for new shipping. In Canada we have magnificent opportunities for shipbuilding. I remember, when I was a comparatively young man, when in the province of New Brunswick there were dozens of shipyards turning out magnificent wooden ships which sailed upon every sea and carried the fame and reputation of our province to all parts of the world.
